schools.summary: Gill canvasses the chronologies, reporting Josephus for Eli and the Jewish reckoning for the days of Eglon and Ehud, and notes that the name Elimelech suits an age whose government was a theocracy.

Henry reads the date devotionally, that while the judges ruled Providence took particular cognizance of Bethlehem with an eye to a King descended from two Gentile mothers, and cites bishop Patrick for Gideon on the ground of a famine caused by invasion.

Clarke lists the candidate judges without disguising the confusion and defines the book as an appendix containing a perfect history in itself, useful in the Gospels for ascertaining the line by which Christ came; Wesley compresses the whole question into the descent from Rahab.

Ellicott renders the phrase as when the judges judged and warns the note of time is by no means definite; Keil and Delitzsch read the five names as genuine Hebrew and judge the Moabitess names to resist the same treatment.

debates.question: When in the period of the judges does the story fall?
debates.positions: Gill reports Josephus for Eli and rejects it as too late for Boaz to be the grandfather of Jesse, preferring the Jewish chronology at Eglon and Ehud, with Lightfoot broadly agreeing; Clarke reports that Usher settled on Shamgar and most chronologers followed; Henry and Ellicott reason from the genealogy that it must be early because Boaz was the son of Rahab; Henry adds Patrick for Gideon.

debates.question: Can the Moabitess names be etymologised like the Hebrew ones?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch call the sense of turning the back given to Orpah very arbitrary and the derivation of Ruth from a word for a friend quite uncertain; Clarke and Ellicott render the Hebrew names confidently as sickness and wasting, and Ellicott takes them as given for the boys feeble health and pointing to their early death.

outliers.view: Sees no reasonable ground for supposing the Rahab of the genealogy to be other than the Rahab of Jericho, and uses that identification to date the whole narrative early.
Turns the meaning of the sons names into a proverb about created comforts: such are the products of our pleasant things, weak and infirm, fading and dying.

themes: a famine in the land
the judges judged
names that carry the story
two Gentile mothers
weak and infirm, fading and dying

schools.summary: Gill weighs Josephus against Alshech on whether Elimelech saw his sons married, carries the Targum verdict that they transgressed the decree of the Word of the Lord, and alone looks past the question of guilt to the providence by which the Messiah might spring from one of these women.

Clarke endorses the Targum as proper and thinks there is more here than conjecture; Wesley states the alternatives without choosing, that either they were proselytes when they married or the sons sinned and were punished with short life and want of issue, and ends on the question by whom a woman thus bereaved shall be comforted.

Ellicott reads the marriages as a second step down from the fathers first, declines to say how far those are right who see the deaths as punishment, and treats the two names and the Targum claim that Ruth was a daughter of Eglon as questions of evidence.

debates.question: Were the marriages to Moabite women lawful?
debates.positions: Gill reports Aben Ezra that the women were proselytes before the match and thinks it plainly so of Ruth at least, but sets against it the Targum verdict of transgression, noting that some writers excuse and others condemn; Clarke endorses the Targum; Ellicott calls the marriages a further risk of being drawn into idolatry, as a later and greater king found; Wesley leaves both alternatives standing.

debates.question: Were the three deaths a judgement?
debates.positions: Gill and Clarke both carry the Targum that because the sons joined in affinity with a strange people their days were cut off, Clarke adding that it is very likely more than conjecture; Ellicott will not go so far, saying only that they died clearly as quite young men and that it is not for us to say how far such readings are right.

outliers.view: Alone converts the dispute over the marriages into providence, that however it was, the thing was so permitted and ordered that from one of these women the Messiah might spring.
Reports the Targum making Ruth the daughter of Eglon king of Moab and ascribes it to an obvious wish to exalt her dignity.

themes: three men in three verses
strange wives
the Word of the Lord
left alone of her two sons and her husband
by whom shall she be comforted

schools.summary: Gill sharpens her motive to the better opportunities of serving the Lord her own country afforded, notes that the text says the field of Moab rather than any city, reads the setting out as an escort only, and collects the older attempts to supply the elliptical blessing.

Henry makes the verse a portrait of affection for the land she had left, which she could not stay in while the famine lasted and would not stay out of once it ceased, and reads the visitation as mercy: though God contend long he will not contend always.

Clarke collects the Targum additions, that she heard by the mouth of an angel and that the visitation came for the righteousness of Ibzan and the supplications of pious Boaz; Wesley glosses bread as food and explains the mothers house from the custom by which daughters conversed more with their mothers in separate apartments.

Ellicott reads both women as purposing to go the whole way and calls the dismissal wholly unselfish, hearing a twofold blessing made solemn by naming the covenant God twice; Keil and Delitzsch make the grammar carry the distinction, that the word return applies strictly only to Naomi.

debates.question: How far did the daughters-in-law mean to go?
debates.positions: Gill reads it as an escort only, placing the parting at the utmost limits of Moab on the borders of Israel and doubting any intention to enter Canaan; Ellicott reads them as clearly purposing to go with Naomi to the land of Israel, since a parting then could hardly be anything but final; Keil and Delitzsch settle it grammatically, that return strictly applies only to Naomi while the others merely wished to accompany her.

debates.question: Does the blessing need a supplement?
debates.positions: Gill records the Targum filling it out as a perfect reward, Aben Ezra as a husband and Josephus as happier marriages than they had made with her sons, but thinks no supplement needed since what follows is the sum of the wish; Ellicott simply hears two blessings, mercy in general and the particular mercy of rest in a new home.

outliers.view: Thinks it not without probability that Mahlon and Chilion are the two men named elsewhere as having married in Moab.
Reports the supposition, from the text saying field rather than city, that the family were either not permitted to dwell in the towns or chose not to, the better to avoid their neighbours idolatry.
Explains the mothers house rather than the fathers, though Ruths father was living, because a mothers love knows best how to comfort a daughter in her affliction.

themes: the LORD had visited his people in giving them bread
the field of Moab
the mothers house
rest in the house of her husband
they lifted up their voice and wept

schools.summary: Gill reads the dissuasion as a probe of motive, suspecting their resolution sprang from natural affection only, and notes how far the supposition has to be stretched to be refused at all.

Clarke lays the address out in its steps and admires it as he goes; Wesley grounds it in the ancient custom and express statute Naomi had doubtless acquainted them with, and finds the right posture under the closing clause, that we are to hear the voice of the rod as if it spoke to us alone.

Keil and Delitzsch spell out the levirate logic that there are no younger brothers to carry the obligation; Ellicott watches the effect rather than the argument and judges a different rendering of the last clause much more probable on the versions.

debates.question: How should the last clause of Naomi speech be rendered?
debates.positions: The received text and Wesley take it as grief for their sakes, and Wesley lists what grieves her, including circumstances so mean that Ruth would shortly be gleaning for a living; Ellicott judges it much more probable that it means it is far more bitter for me than for you, citing an exact parallel of construction with the Septuagint, the Peshito Syriac and the Targum supporting it and only the Vulgate rendering loosely.

debates.question: Was Naomi trying to send them back or to test them?
debates.positions: Gill takes the whole speech as a probe, to find out whether either was moved by religion at bottom and to prevent a later apostasy that would reproach the true religion; Ellicott reads it as genuine dissuasion whose advice proves insufficient to shake their affectionate resolve, at which point she turns from their prospects to her own loneliness.

outliers.view: Reads the speech as a contrast of lots rather than an argument: they are young and may go forth to homes of their own, while she is old, childless and solitary and must wend her weary way back unaided.

Turns the clause into a rule for the afflicted, that though many share a trouble we are to hear the voice of the rod as if it spoke to us alone, and warns against setting the hand to the plough and looking back.

themes: surely we will return with thee unto thy people
are there yet any more sons in my womb
too old to have an husband
the hand of the LORD is gone out against me
setting the hand to the plough

schools.summary: Gill reads the second weeping as the sound of women who cannot bear the thought of parting, and takes the whole dissuasion as the steadfastness Naomi wanted to make trial of.
Henry makes Orpah the warning and Ruth the contrary example, of the grace of God inclining the soul to choose the better part.

Clarke notes the Septuagint addition that Orpah returned to her own people and judges both women probably idolaters whose conversion had not yet begun; Wesley reads the kiss as a farewell for ever and hears the appeal to her gods as a warning that forsaking the communion of saints breaks off communion with God.
Ellicott explains Orpah by the hardships of the journey and of its end, and criticises Naomi own theology; Keil and Delitzsch set out the text of the exchange and the oath formula that closes it.

debates.question: Were Orpah and Ruth idolaters or already proselytes?
debates.positions: Clarke says they were probably both idolaters, that the conjecture of their having been proselytes is unfounded, that Chemosh was the grand idol of the Moabites, and that Ruth conversion probably commenced at this moment; Wesley assumes Naomi had already taught them the true religion and reads her words as intimating that to come she must embrace it.

debates.question: Was Naomi urging Ruth back in earnest?
debates.positions: Wesley and Gill both read it as a test of sincerity and constancy; Ellicott reads it as a fresh argument pressed in earnest, Naomi being newly armed by Orpah example.

outliers.view: Faults Naomi theology rather than Ruth resolve, holding that she views the Moabite idols as realities whose power is confined to the land of Moab and is not sufficiently enlightened to see in the Lord more than the God of Israel.
Uses Orpah in almost the same words as Wesley, that many have a value for Christ yet come short of salvation by him because they will not forsake other things for him.

themes: Orpah kissed her mother in law
but Ruth clave unto her
gone back unto her people and unto her gods
they love him yet leave him
choose the better part

schools.summary: Gill lingers on the verb of the first clause, reading it as do not meet me or be against me, and presses the burial clause to the same country, cottage, bed and grave, marking that she has no regard at all to the sepulchres of her fathers.

Clarke calls it the most perfect surrender of friendly feelings ever made, sets the Targum catechetical expansion beside it, records that Ruth kept the oath as nurse to Obed in the house of Boaz, and refuses to describe the divining practice attached to the verse; Wesley reads the burial clause as joined souls mingling dust and makes resolution the bolt on a door that would otherwise invite a thief.

Keil and Delitzsch identify the closing words as a fixed formula used in swearing and render the verb of verse eighteen as stiffening oneself firmly upon a thing; Ellicott observes that the intensity comes out more strongly now she pleads alone and that taken literally she swears by the name of the God of Israel.

debates.question: What is the force of the closing words of Ruth vow?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch treat them as a stock oath formula by which the speaker calls down a severe punishment on himself if he should not keep his word, citing parallels; Ellicott treats them as a solemn oath specific to this moment in which, taken literally, Ruth swears by the name of the God of Israel; Clarke reads them as an imprecation she afterwards made good.

outliers.view: Reports that the verse is famous among those who strive to divine by the Bible, declines to relate the particulars lest he prolong the practice, and says he saw it done in his youth and was terrified.
Suggests the Targum catechetical dialogue reflects real practice, that some such conversation likely took place between the elders and those who were becoming proselytes.
Reaches for classical parallels of friends buried in one grave, and notes that Ruth surrenders the sepulchres of her fathers, which people in all ages and countries have been fond of being laid in.

themes: whither thou goest I will go
thy people shall be my people
the house of burial
a door ajar which invites a thief
then she left speaking unto her

schools.summary: Gill has them go straight on and keep together, Ruth walking at her ancient mothers pace and edified by her conversation, and notices the absence of camels, asses and servants as the measure of their mean circumstances.

Henry allows both compassion and contempt in the crowd, calls the upbraiding temper base and sordid, argues from the notice taken of her that she had formerly lived respectably, and carries the change in three images.
Clarke reads the commotion as respect and infers that Elimelech was of high consideration in the place; Wesley puts the townswomens question in a single line about plenty and honour changed.

Keil and Delitzsch settle the speakers from the feminine verbs and locate the amazement in the manner of her return rather than the fact of it; Ellicott measures the journey at not less than fifty miles across two rivers and notes that news of her had not reached Bethlehem.

debates.question: In what spirit did the city ask, Is this Naomi?
debates.positions: Clarke reads the commotion as simple respect for a well known and highly regarded family; Keil and Delitzsch read amazement at her mournful condition as a solitary widow; Ellicott reads neighbourly excitement at a woman they never looked to see again; Henry allows all of these and a fourth, contempt, which he condemns as barbarous while judging that most asked in commiseration.

outliers.view: Reaches for three figures of a reversed condition in one breath: the gold become dim, the rose withered and unlike itself blooming, and those who had seen the magnificence of the first temple weeping at the meanness of the second.
Notes the asymmetry of news, that word of the end of the famine reached Naomi in Moab while no word of her had reached Bethlehem.

themes: so they two went
all the city was moved about them
is this Naomi
how is the gold become dim
weary and travel-stained

schools.summary: Gill cites Josephus for the two names then declines to depend on him, reports and rejects the Jewish charge of covetousness against the family, and reads the closing verse as the writers own note to excite the attention of the reader.
Henry makes the plainer point about the season, that they came seasonably, and that our times are in Gods hand, both the events and the time of them.

Clarke glosses the names, reads Shaddai as the self-sufficient who has taken away the props of her life, supposes Elimelech carried property into Moab on which Naomi subsisted until it was spent, dates the harvest to the beginning of spring after the passover, and argues from the amiable simplicity of the story to its genuineness; Wesley fills out the fulness and reads the last verb judicially.

Ellicott treats the renaming as one of the constant plays upon words and names in the Hebrew Bible, denies any connection between Mara and Miriam or Mary, reads Shaddai as the God who gives all things in abundance and therefore takes back, and dates barley harvest to about the end of April; Keil and Delitzsch supply the text of the three verses.

debates.question: When does the beginning of barley harvest fall?
debates.positions: Clarke places it in the beginning of spring, immediately after the passover on the fifteenth of the month, nearly answering to our March, and adds the Targum claim that they arrived on the very day the sheaf was first mown to be waved before the Lord; Ellicott, calling barley the earliest harvest, places it ordinarily about the end of April.

debates.question: Was the family culpable for going to Moab?
debates.positions: Gill reports Jewish writers, Jarchi among them, blaming Elimelech and Naomi for going abroad at such a time out of a covetous disposition and an unwillingness to relieve the poor, and being punished for it, then rejects the charge as said without any just cause or reason that appears; Clarke offers the neutral explanation that a man fleeing famine would naturally carry his property with him.

outliers.view: Declines to depend on Josephus for the sense of the two names, on the ground that he is not always correct in his interpretation of Hebrew words.
Pauses on a popular etymology to deny it, that Mara has no connection with Miriam or Mary, which come from a different root.
Argues from manner to genuineness, that the amiable simplicity of the narrative contains sympathetic circumstances no forger could have invented, too much of nature to admit anything of art.
Notes Aben Ezra taking the closing verse of a return at some other time, against his own reading of it as the historians summary.

themes: call me not Naomi call me Mara
I went out full
the Almighty hath afflicted me
the beginning of barley harvest
the sheaf waved before the Lord
